doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Music everywhere, Brazil and jazz as export
summary: Discussing ubiquitous music, he praises Brazilian street music and the favela matchbox player and sees jazz as an export into other people's music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: It’s interesting you say that. I wonder, you know in some sense music is all over the place, and sometimes I wonder if it’s too much. Like it’s in the grocery stores, you can’t avoid it when you’re walking down the street because someone’s blaring it out of their car. And after a while it becomes not as special.

Yeah. Well you know one thing? The strongest thing about that is a place like Brazil. Now you know I’m going to be guilty of saying good music and bad music, because most of the time in the grocery stores and stuff you’re hearing bad music, I feel that anyhow. This is my opinion. And you hear elevator music, music with the drums etched out, or somebody in their car and you’re not even hearing music you’re hearing something going boom-boom and the car’s jumping up and down. Where in Brazil you hear a Samba all the time. All the time. [scats] And you hear a guitarist. But the guitars are playing the most beautiful changes, even if it’s some kid just sitting in Sao Paulo somewhere with no legs and playing the guitar, he’s playing these gorgeous changes and stuff. He’s not just going [scats]. And in Brazil it is, it’s infectious. You talk about hearing it all the time, it’s a way of life, it’s the sound of the cities, the sound of Sao Paulo, and it’s everywhere. It’s just like you can hear the traffic, you can hear everything, but you hear it [scats] and it’s totally amazing. I’ll never forget in Brazil going to one of these favelas they have up in the hills and they don’t have like bars and stuff it’s like somebody has this great big box or something and he’s there and people just come up, it’s like a street bar. It’s not enclosed all the way. But I was in one of those clubs, and everybody’s playing this, they’ve got maracas and everybody jams and stuff. And one guy had a matchbox, one of those little wooden matchboxes with some of the matches taken out of it, and he’s going chic-a-chica-a-chica-a-chica. But he was like a virtuoso. And then he would take his fingers and go [scats] and he’s doing all this stuff with them. And then everybody gives each other five and a bunch of other guys will come in and start doing it. And of course drinking. They had this drink that was amazing. A sasha or something, it was like a lot of alcohol and a lot of sugar is how I remember. You would get stoned off this thing. But I mean jazz music, I just see it now as you know it’s always going to be an element in American music, it’s been such a strong statement from the beginning. But I see the jazz as salvation out of America. I mean it’s — what do you call it — this intrusion into other people’s music all over the world, it’s the most exciting thing I feel that jazz is doing.
Yeah. It’s a great export for this country.
Do you have any interesting plans in the near future?
